speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In May this year, I informed the House that a Committee of Inquiry (COI) would be convened to investigate the death of full-time National Serviceman Corporal (First Class) (CFC) Dave Lee that occurred on 30 April 2018.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Under the SAF Act, the COI is structured primarily to investigate and determine facts related to the incident and to identify causation, lapses and systemic problems, if any, which resulted in the incident.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI does not deal with culpability of individuals.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Specifically, to encourage disclosure and cooperation by all involved in the incident, section 8C of the SAF Act provides that no statements made to the COI shall be admissible as evidence in a Court Martial or for disciplinary proceedings.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: To keep to this remit, I will, therefore, use no names nor designations in this Statement but instead use a generic term – commander/s or person/s, as appropriate.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As I mentioned in May to this House, Police investigations are ongoing and the Coroner may hold an inquiry.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Their procedures and evidence uncovered are part of the judicial process to determine if any criminal offence has been committed in this incident and are separate from the COI.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In May, I had also informed this House that the COI would submit its report to the External Review Panel on SAF Safety (ERPSS).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI has done so for their preliminary assessment and I will also be sharing the ERPSS' responses and recommendations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On 17 April this year, CFC Dave Lee and the troopers from the Support Company participated in two physical training sessions in Bedok Camp, namely, Combat Circuit 4 from 6.30 am to 7.30 am at the hockey pitch, and Cardiovascular 6, followed by Balance, Flexibility and Mobility 6 from 3.30 pm to 5.30 pm at the running track.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was a day before the heat stroke.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In this lesson, soldiers had to run six laps of 400 metres each, a total of 2.4 kilometres (km).

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They have to run according to the lesson plan, grouped according to their running ability.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: However, the entire company was asked to run at a common pace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This meant that, for the first three laps, CFC Lee was asked to run at a slightly faster pace than required, of about 10 seconds faster per lap.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For the next three laps, CFC Lee was allowed to run at his own pace.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These deviations were a breach of Training Safety Regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The reason given was that the commanders wanted to enhance fitness and foster greater cohesion by keeping the platoon intact, and the soldiers running at the same pace, not in groups.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At about 9.40 pm, the entire Scout Platoon, including CFC Lee, were told to fall-in in their No 4 uniforms and assault bags.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The commander/s had wanted to punish the platoon collectively for the perceived lack of teamwork and the use of mobile phones after Lights Out, in particular, by two troopers, despite repeated warnings.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At 9.45 pm, the commander/s meted out the informal punishment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was in the form of physical exercises, which comprised Bear Crawls, Sprints, Leopard Crawls, as well as Push-Ups and Crunches.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In total, it was from 30 to 35 minutes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They also had water poured over the troopers from their water bottles and subsequently from the jerry can.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The session ended with the troopers reciting the Guards Creed a few times in a high kneel position.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As I have said, the entire session lasted for about 30 to 35 minutes.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The platoon was eventually sent back to their bunks at about 10.25 pm to wash up and had Lights Out by 10.45 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The troopers were also instructed by commanders not to switch on the lights in their bunks.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI noted that the commanders did not seek prior approval for the conduct of this informal punishment or inform their superiors after the punishment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: While the majority of the troopers interviewed opined that the commanders were good commanders who demanded high standards, this punishment was unauthorised.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Less sleep could be one of the factors which caused CFC Lee to have more fatigue before participating in the fast march.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI's assessment was that the conduct of the fast march was in line with the lesson plan and relevant regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: CFC Lee had undergone the requisite build-up training prior to the eight-km fast march, and all measures to prevent heat injuries according to the TSR had been complied with – which are temperature-taking regime, hydration regime, water supply where soldiers must carry water and have resupply points planned for, work-rest cycle based on the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature, and rest management, except that CFC Lee and his platoon did not have the requisite seven hours of sleep that I have just mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Before the fast march, CFC Lee had taken his temperature, which was normal at 36.3°C, and had drunk water.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was witnessed by his buddy, who also observed him to be looking well and seemed to be his usual self.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: CFC Lee and his fellow scout troopers then consumed their Recommended Dietary Allowance, which consisted of an oatmeal cracker and chrysanthemum drink.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Thereafter, the safety brief was conducted by the Conducting Officer.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Troopers were asked if they had completed their six-km fast march build-up training, completed their water parade, and had seven hours of uninterrupted rest, and taken their body temperature during the declaration.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The troops were asked to declare if they had.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Conducting Officer had checked if there was anyone who was not feeling well.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Three troopers stood out as they had not completed their six-km fast march and were subsequently deployed as marshals.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: No one else sounded off any other concerns when the checks were made.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was followed by the conduct of warm-up exercises to get the troopers ready for the eight-km fast march.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: After the conduct of warm-up exercises, the fast march commenced just before sunrise with the troopers despatched in four waves, at five-minute intervals.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Each wave included a commander as a rear sweeper.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: CFC Lee was in the fourth wave – the last wave.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: After CFC Lee completed the first six km, he had a mandated 20-minute rest.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: After the 20-minute rest period, as CFC Lee was moving off for the last two km, he sounded off to the commanders that he had cramps in his calf muscles.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: They advised him to stretch his calf muscles, which he did, and encouraged him to complete the march.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Shortly after the fast march, as CFC Lee was walking from the end point of the fast march to the Support Company line, he was observed to be disoriented and immediately attended to by the commander/s and the cover medic/s.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: After the fast march, the persons attending to CFC Lee thought that he was suffering from physical exhaustion.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: His pulse was assessed to be normal and his skin felt cold to touch.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When his condition did not improve, CFC Lee was subsequently evacuated to the medical centre.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: However, there was a significant gap between the onset of symptoms and his arrival at the medical centre.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: On arrival at the Bedok Camp Medical Centre, CFC Lee was semi-conscious.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Two bags of fast IV drip were administered and he was also placed in the Body Cooling Unit, for two cycles.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Seeing that CFC Lee was not responding to the treatment, the Medical Officer decided to evacuate him to the Changi General Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Medical Officer accompanied CFC Lee in the SAF ambulance to Changi General Hospital’s Accident and Emergency (A&E) department where he was handed over and admitted to the Intensive Care Unit.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The COI opined that the significant delay from the time of symptoms to evacuation could have escalated the heat injury to a heat stroke.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Full body cooling should have been instituted as soon as possible and within 30 minutes of presentation of signs and symptoms.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The delay in evacuation resulted as the persons attending to CFC Lee mistook his signs and symptoms as being due to physical exhaustion.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Though trained, they had never encountered any previous case of heat injury themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There were several suggestions for CFC Lee to be evacuated, but these calls were either not heard or not heeded.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For completeness, let me share the COI’s finding on one other aspect, which is CFC Lee’s state of health prior to the fast march.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: While CFC Lee had no significant medical history, it was established that he had been taking some medication in the weeks prior to the fast march following a visit to the Jurong Polyclinic on 31 March 2018 for acute upper respiratory tract infection.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was more than two weeks before the fast march on 18 April.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Other than this, the COI did not find any physical injury sustained, as verified by the autopsy, nor any evidence indicating any foul play or medical negligence that caused his death.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) will await the outcome of the Police investigations and Coroner’s Inquiry, as well as the Attorney-General’s Chambers' decision whether to prosecute any persons in the criminal Court.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: If no criminal charges are filed, MINDEF will prosecute persons responsible for lapses in this incident in our military Court.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, the ERPSS agreed with the COI’s preliminary assessment on the cause of death, as earlier stated.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, the panel emphasised that it is essential for personnel to comply with safety rules promulgated in the approved operating manuals.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Breaches, such as those found by the COI in this case, should not be condoned.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, the ERPSS highlighted the value of strengthening the safety culture in Army units.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: They felt that if each soldier takes greater personal ownership and responsibility for safety, it would bring about desirable behaviours, such as (a) having a strong respect for safety rules and guidelines; (b) being willing to speak out when there are safety concerns; (c) taking care of one another; and (d) open-reporting, so as to share lessons and prevent future accidents.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Such behaviours would substantially strengthen the Army’s efforts to ensure safe training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: First, the need to strengthen commanders’ knowledge on heat injuries and improve their decision-making processes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, for medics to be able to exercise their professional authority when dealing with medical issues.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This includes being able to communicate effectively with commanders who are much more senior than them.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Third, for commanders to watch out for soldiers who are feeling unwell or are unable to cope and proactively pull them out of training before they get injured.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI will submit its final report after completion of the Police investigations and Coroner’s Inquiry, if held.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Training and safety protocols were reviewed and advised by an External Review Panel on Heat Injury Management (ERPHIM).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This was chaired by Assoc Prof Mark Leong, who is a senior consultant at the Department of Emergency Medicine at the Singapore General Hospital (SGH).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The following changes will be put into place.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This takes the guesswork out of the assessment and what the reason is, as this case showed, and imposes early evacuation as the default, as a strict Training Safety Regulation to be followed.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Second, additional methods to cool servicemen during training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Portable cooling methods, such as purpose-built cooling pads, will now replace less effective ice packs, to be used on the spot.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These will be implemented in phases, starting from this month.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The expert opinion of this Expert Review Panel on Heat Injuries is that those currently available in the market are not effective for measuring core temperature.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fourth, the Army will ensure that our commanders and soldiers can better recognise the signs and symptoms of heat injuries.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Fifth, the importance of open reporting will be emphasised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Soldiers will be encouraged to use the Hotline to report any unauthorised activities or violations of rules, especially during Basic Military Training phase and reinforced during In-Camp Training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Army will encourage our soldiers not to push themselves beyond safety limits.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If a soldier feels that he is unwell during any training activity, or if the buddy notices it, soldiers will be reminded to err on the side of caution, to stop and make up training another day.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Seventh, more clinical exposure and patient contacts for medics to upgrade their skills in resuscitation and handling of emergencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This may include periodic attachments to hospitals, A&E departments or to run in ambulances.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: CFC Lee was an exemplary soldier who served with commitment, and was well-respected by his peers for his positive attitude.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The loss of such a good soldier like CFC Lee is deeply grievous to us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It will take collective effort to achieve zero training fatalities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Each serviceman must take care of himself or sound the alert when his buddy is not well, or if regulations are not complied with during training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Commanders must be alert and pull out early those who are not coping and use another occasion to train.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Zero training deaths must be the norm and any mishap should be vigorously attended to by commanders to achieve this norm.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I assure all Members that MINDEF and the SAF will do all it can to help the family through this difficult period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And if they did not respond that they did not have seven hours of uninterrupted sleep, how do we, in future, make sure that the soldiers would state the truth of the matter?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do we ensure that, in their zeal, perhaps, soldiers take cognisance and take training safety regulations seriously?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I presume that some of them who did not have seven hours uninterrupted sleep, for instance, still said, "I can go on".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said, this was the external safety review panel's comment, too, that you have got to make it second nature for the trainees to say, "Look, this is for my own self-protection or my buddy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I am going to tell on you because you did not do it, because I am going to protect you." We thought that one crucial factor was to give more opportunities for make-up training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if they know they have time to make up and they would not fail the course, there will be more incentives for them to declare that they did not have it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if commanders know now that if the conditions are not met, they will ensure that the conditions are met.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is not going to be an easy answer.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At this stage of ours where we have the regulations but we are not sure everybody follows these, we need everybody to play their part to achieve zero training fatalities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Did any of his colleagues or instructors detect or spot that he was not coping well during the training?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second question is: would the SAF look into the possibility of training commanders for early detection of soldiers who are not coping well during an extreme, strenuous exercise like the fast march so that they can be pulled out before the completion of the fast march?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the first six km, there did not seem to be any witness who noticed anything out of the ordinary.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During the last two km, he complained of cramps, told his commanders and his commanders advised him to stretch, which he did.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And he was the last one to complete the fast march.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was only at the end of the fast march as he was walking towards the company line that they noticed that he was disoriented and then, the medics and others gave him immediate attention.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: How do we ensure better recognition by commanders and men?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, as I have said, one of the recommendations is to take the guesswork out of this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this instance, those attending to him thought he had physical exhaustion, not heat exhaustion.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we have learnt from this that, you do not guess, you may not be in the best position, err on the side of caution.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we want a simple mechanism where you can determine if someone is disoriented.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the Report, I do not sense that the weather was a factor for this heat injury.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, yes, indeed, temperature is taken into account.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In fact, after this, we looked around other militaries to see whether we were more stringent or less stringent than others.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, different militaries use different work-rest cycles depending on what the temperature or the humidity is.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But it is not a discretion given to commanders.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the next steps are all quite logical.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But one of the things that struck me – this was a trainee who, for all intents and purposes, appeared healthy to everyone, even completed the exercise and then passed out after that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are many situations where tough training pushes people to the limits.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, are there any thoughts about looking at exercise-specific instructions?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, if you are doing, say, trench-digging, where you would not sleep for a number of nights, you might be a little bit tired; you might be a little bit disoriented.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But does that require the same procedures – what is normal, what is not?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And maybe something more attuned to specific exercises, particularly those that are higher, I guess, that test people more, may be useful as well because it will probably be different in different exercises.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The approach that the Army uses is graduation – in other words, graduated activities that train up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if you notice from my Ministerial Statement, one of the prerequisites that the conducting officer had asked was: have all of you done the six-km march?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And some did not, alerted themselves and fell out of the march.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, there was graduation, and not only in terms of just distance but tolerance for heat.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that is also built into the programme.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I would say at our level that we have not had a heat stroke of this magnitude for the last nine years, as I have said.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Unfortunately, the commanders, those who dealt with CFC Lee had never encountered one in their own experience and that may have been part of the problem.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But for every activity, as Mr Vikram Nair pointed out, we want to make sure that the trainees are built up to take higher levels of activity, and that is the prevailing principle and practice.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: I am not sure if I understood correctly, is it true to say that the conclusion is that CFC Lee's condition and the six-km march could not be linked to what happened to him subsequently?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Did the COI actually give any conclusions about whether there was a link?

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: My second clarification is: I think the Minister said earlier that wearables were considered but have now been ruled out.

speaker: Assoc Prof Randolph Tan (Nominated Member)
text: Would the possible use of wearables continue to be explored?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Other than this, they did not find any physical injury sustained nor any foul play or medical negligence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Heat stroke is usually a culmination of events – exposure to heat, your own body's mechanisms cannot cope with the heat produced and it shuts down.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The COI opined that they could not find any direct cause but it could have been due to a number of accumulated causes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But they felt that his succumbing to the heat stroke was a result of delay between the symptoms and evacuation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I think the Member's second question was on wearables.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We had an expert panel of doctors – the Chair, who is a senior consultant in the A&E Department in SGH – and they concluded that wearables that are on the market do not measure core temperature that well because, for heat injuries or heat strokes, you need to measure core temperature.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In this case, as Members have noticed, when they touched CFC Lee's skin, it was actually cold, cooler than norm – it was not warm.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if you have wearables that measure surface temperature, it does not quite work.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You have to measure core temperature, and the technology just is not there yet.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The first clarification is the part about the conducting officer asking them if they had seven hours of rest.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The troop apparently did not respond to that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Did the COI talk about why they did not respond to that?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Was there a reason why they did not?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The second question is, I wonder if there is a daily log of the activities that the troops go through that would have been recorded every day so that that would include how many hours of rest that they have or any extra activities that have been added on.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Is there such a daily log that has been placed so that we could check on it, at least, for the conducting officer?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I would have to go back to the detailed COI Report to see whether they had asked the various platoon members why they did not all say they did not have the seven hours of sleep.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: From what I can recollect, they did not give specific reasons.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And as I have said, one surmises that they wanted to do it because they wanted to carry on with their training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As I have said earlier in my Statement, the commanders who conducted the informal punishment neither sought permission nor told their superiors of this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, I think, this was missed – the seven hours – they did not have the requisite seven hours of sleep.
